lead: Bleed air is compressed air taken from an engine compressor and used, after regulation, as the aircraft's clean source of pressure and heat. Instead of carrying a separate compressor for every job, the aircraft taps air the engine has already compressed. That air drives cabin cooling and pressurisation, clears ice from the wing and intake, and spins the engine during start. This chapter follows the air from the bleed port to the users, and names the valves and protections that keep pressure and temperature inside safe limits.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for how valves and actuators are driven, and Chapter 2.6 for what happens to the air after it leaves the manifold.

blocks.text: An engine compressor raises the pressure and temperature of air before combustion. A small fraction of that air is taken out through a bleed port and sent to the aircraft. This is cheaper than carrying a separate compressor for cabin air, and the air is already hot and dry. Pressure at the port depends on which compressor stage is tapped and on engine power. A low-pressure (LP) port gives cooler air at moderate pressure. A high-pressure (HP) port gives higher pressure but hotter air.

At low engine power the LP stage cannot supply enough pressure. The HP valve opens and HP air feeds the system. As power rises, LP pressure becomes enough; the HP valve closes and a check valve stops HP air from flowing backwards into the LP duct. So the source switches with power, and bleed is not always available from the HP stage.

Three sources feed the manifold: engine bleed (HP or LP), the auxiliary power unit (APU) on the ground and during engine start, and a ground cart connected at a ground service port. Before cooling, bleed air may sit at a few hundred kPa and a few hundred degrees Celsius. One kPa is 1000 Pa, and 100 kPa is about one atmosphere.

The first heat exchanger is the precooler. Fan air passes on one side and hot bleed on the other. The precooler lowers the bleed temperature, but the air leaving it is still hot enough to need heat protection on ducts. A fan-air valve controls the cooling flow.

Next is the pressure regulating and shut-off valve (PRV). The PRV regulates the downstream pressure to a design value, usually a few hundred kPa, and can close fully to shut off the bleed. It is controlled by a bleed monitoring computer that reads pressure and temperature sensors in the duct.

The regulated air enters a manifold: a network of ducts that runs along the fuselage. Check valves allow flow from a source into the manifold but block reverse flow, so a failed engine bleed cannot pressurise another engine's ducts. Isolation valves split the manifold into sections. If one section leaks, the crew can close an isolation valve and keep the other engine supplying the remaining users.

Protection is layered. For overpressure, the PRV closes and a relief valve opens if the PRV fails. For overheat, duct sensors trip a warning and close the affected valve. The crew sees the fault on the bleed panel or the electronic centralised aircraft monitor (ECAM), depending on the aircraft.
The manifold feeds several users, each through its own valve:

items: Air conditioning packs take bleed air and cool it; the air cycle machine is covered in Chapter 2.6.
Wing and engine anti-ice use hot bleed air to keep surfaces above freezing; see Chapter 2.11.
Engine starting uses bleed air to turn the starter; see Chapter 2.5.
Hydraulic reservoirs and water tanks are pressurised with bleed air to prevent pump cavitation and to supply water.
Some door seals inflate with bleed air.

blocks.text: The packs supply conditioned air to the cabin; the outflow valve then controls cabin altitude. Cabin pressure is a downstream result of pack air, not a separate bleed-fed user.

On a typical twin-engine aircraft, either engine can supply the whole manifold through the isolation valves. The APU supplies the manifold on the ground when engines are off; its air joins downstream of the precooler and the PRV, so no engine fan air is needed to cool it. This shared manifold is why a single bleed leak can affect several systems, and why isolation valves matter.

blocks.where: ṁ is mass flow in kg/s, ρ is air density in kg/m³, A is duct cross-section area in m², and v is mean velocity in m/s.

spec.title: Typical air pressure system
spec.aria: Engine bleed passes through a precooler and a pressure regulating valve into the manifold. APU bleed joins the manifold downstream of these through its own shut-off valve and check valve. The manifold supplies the air conditioning packs, anti-ice and engine start.

examples.question: A bleed duct carries 0.30 kg/s of air at 250 kPa and 200 °C. The duct area is 0.010 m². Take R = 287 J/(kg·K). Find the air density and the mean velocity.
steps: Convert temperature to kelvin: T = 200 + 273 = 473 K.
Convert pressure to pascal: p = 250 kPa = 250 000 Pa.
Apply the ideal-gas relation: ρ = p/(R × T) = 250 000/(287 × 473).
Use mass flow: ṁ = ρ × A × v, so v = ṁ/(ρ × A).
examples.answer: The density is 1.84 kg/m³ and the mean velocity is 16.29 m/s.
examples.check:
p = 250000.0
T = 473.0
R = 287.0
mdot = 0.30
A = 0.010
rho = p/(R*T)
v = mdot/(rho*A)
print(round(rho, 2))
print(round(v, 2))

traps: Bleed is always available: at low engine power only the HP stage can supply it; the HP valve closes again at high power. Do not assume the HP port is the normal source at cruise.
Confusing the precooler with the air cycle machine. The precooler is a fan-air heat exchanger before the manifold; the air cycle machine is inside the pack and cools by expansion.
Using gauge pressure instead of absolute pressure in ρ = p/(RT). The formula needs absolute pressure in Pa and absolute temperature in K.
Thinking the isolation valve is a check valve. A check valve is one-way and automatic; an isolation valve is opened or closed by command to split the manifold.
Forgetting that overheat protection closes the bleed valve, not the pack valve.

quiz.q: Name the two engine compressor bleed sources.
quiz.a: The low-pressure (LP) stage and the high-pressure (HP) stage.

quiz.q: Why is a precooler fitted before the manifold?
quiz.a: It uses fan air to reduce the bleed temperature so ducts and valves are not overheated; the air is still hot after it.

quiz.q: A duct carries 0.24 kg/s of air of density 1.80 kg/m³ through an area of 0.008 m². Find the mean velocity.
Why does the HP bleed valve close at high engine power?
quiz.a: At high power the LP stage pressure is already enough. Closing the HP valve avoids taking hot, high-pressure air unnecessarily and prevents reverse flow through the HP path.

quiz.q: What is the job of an isolation valve in the bleed manifold?
quiz.a: It splits the manifold into sections so a leak or failed source can be isolated while the other engine supplies the remaining users.

quiz.q: Name three users of bleed air.
quiz.a: Any three: air conditioning packs, anti-ice, engine starting, hydraulic reservoir pressurisation, water tank pressurisation, door seals.

quiz.q: A duct overheat warning appears. What does the bleed system do, and why?
quiz.a: The duct sensor trips a warning and the affected bleed valve closes, stopping hot air from reaching the overheated section.

beyond: Not for the exam. Newer aircraft such as the Boeing 787 use a bleedless architecture: electric compressors make cabin air, and engine bleed is used far less. Research moves toward more-electric aircraft, where hydraulic and pneumatic loads become electrical. Leak detection in bleed ducts uses loop sensors and health monitoring. Search terms: bleedless architecture, bleed monitoring computer, engine bleed leakage, more-electric aircraft.
